newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade transport drivers stage pre-polls strike.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade transport drivers stage pre-polls strike.

text.p: Striking bus and tram drivers stranded thousands of commuters in Belgrade on Monday in a protest over unpaid wages, less than a week before Yugoslavia's federal elections.
"There are only 483 vehicles on the streets today out of 1,009 scheduled," said Slobodan Vucenovic, a dispatcher for the Belgrade public transport company.
"People are angry, I know. But we managed to cover the busiest lines," he told Reuters.
With federal and local elections in Yugoslavia set for Sunday, a wave of strikes or threatened strikes has hit the country over the past several weeks.
The unions are protesting high taxes and unpaid wages and have accused company directors of mismanagement.

State media has virtually ignored strike announcements from taxi drivers, private businessmen and lawyers in an attempt to maintain social peace ahead of the November 3 elections in the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.
Belgrade authorities managed to defuse an earlier strike threat from taxi drivers but the lawyers association said it would launch a strike on Monday.
Political analysts say opposition parties hope to capitalise on dissatisfaction among workers and authorities have accused the opposition of encouraging the strikes.
While crowds waited for hours at bus and trams stops, Socialist government-controlled television reported "a smaller number of public transpoort vehicles due to a fuel shortage in the company".
Vucenovic said a public transport trade union blocked some company garages in the early morning hours, preventing vehicles from leaving.
"Exactly 85 drivers' union members blocked three of our garages," he said.
In a city where most residents rely on public transport, the strike meant that many workers arrived late or not at all.
One elderly woman from a Belgrade suburb said it took her three hours and several buses to reach the city centre, a trip which usually takes her half an hour.
"When the buses finally arrive you can't even get in because they are already so crowded," said Milica.
The drivers' trade union last week announced they would strike on October 28 unless company management agreed to hold talks on unpaid wages and faulty vehicles.
Belgrade dailies quoted the president of the trade union Dragoslav Stosic as saying the drivers' demands were minimal and apolitical.
The drivers wanted payment of their salaries for the first half of October, unpaid holiday bonuses and an end to harassment of union members.
